pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 9-10. Count forwards and backwards in steps of powers of 10 (10; 100; 1,000; 10,000; 100,000) from any number up to 1,000,000 — e.g. count on in 10,000s from 462,000; back in 100,000s from 800,000. Each step changes ONE place, generalising the '10/100/1000 more' work to any power-of-ten step, with roll-over across boundaries.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 5): 'count forwards or backwards in steps of powers of 10 for any given number up to 1,000,000'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): builds on 4.NBT.1 place-value structure and skip-counting foundations.
• Operational details — Use a place-value chart / Gattegno chart and a number line: choose a step (which power of 10), and each count changes just that column — until a boundary forces a carry into the next column (e.g. counting in 10,000s past 990,000). Vary the step size and direction; predict the next terms of a sequence. Emphasise which digit ticks and when the roll-over cascades.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9, emerging): counts on/back in a single power of 10 with no boundary. Tier B (age 9-10, secure): counts in any power of 10 to 1,000,000, naming the changing digit. Tier C (age 10, extending): handles roll-over boundaries and continues/predicts mixed sequences.
bestPractices: Name the step as a power of 10 and track which single column ticks each count.
Use a Gattegno chart / number line so the count is seen as one column changing (or cascading at a boundary).
Vary step size and direction (forwards/backwards) and cross boundaries deliberately.
Have children predict the next terms and articulate the rule.
Connect to the ×10 place-value relationship so the steps are structural, not memorised.
keyRepresentations: Gattegno / place-value chart (step ticks one column)
Digit-stepper display showing the changing digit
commonMisconceptions: Changing the wrong column for the chosen step.
Boundary errors when a column rolls over (990,000 + 10,000).
Losing track of direction (counting back but incrementing).
Reverting to counting in ones for large steps.
Not generalising the pattern across different powers of 10.

learn.summary: For ages 9-10: count forwards and backwards in steps of powers of 10 (10; 100; 1,000; 10,000; 100,000) from any starting number up to 1,000,000, generalising earlier '10/100/1,000 more' work. The core insight is that each step changes exactly ONE place-value column — until a column fills and a roll-over (carry) cascades into the next column. Learners choose a step size and direction, track which digit ticks, and handle boundary crossings such as counting in 10,000s past 990,000 (reaching 1,000,000) or 492,000 up to 502,000. Work spans emerging (single power of 10, no boundary), secure (any power of 10 to 1,000,000, naming the changing digit), and extending (roll-over boundaries and predicting mixed sequences).

activities.title: Single-column counting on a place-value chart
feedback: If the wrong column changes (e.g. 462,000 → 463,000 or → 562,000), point to the ten-thousands column on the chart and count again with only that digit moving; check the step size stays a constant ten-thousand each time.
If a learner reverts to counting in ones, re-name the step aloud ('I am adding ten-thousand, so the ten-thousands digit is what changes') and add one whole counter to that column.
If direction is lost (counting back but the digit increases), restate the direction before each step and confirm the number is getting smaller.
activities.rationale: Naming the step as a power of ten and tracking which single column ticks makes the count structural rather than memorised, and connects to the ×10 place-value relationship where each place is ten times the next. A place-value/Gattegno chart or counters let the one-column change be seen and physically enacted.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should 'count forwards or backwards in steps of powers of 10 for any given number up to 1,000,000'.
Place-value structure (each place ten times the next) underlies counting in powers of ten (4.NBT.1).
Counting in powers of ten changes one place at a time with boundary roll-overs, best shown on a Gattegno chart/number line.
learnerActions: Choose a step that is a power of ten (10; 100; 1,000; 10,000; or 100,000) and a direction (forwards or backwards).
Starting from a given number such as 462,000, count on in 10,000s aloud: 462,000 → 472,000 → 482,000 → 492,000, each time saying which single column changed.
On a place-value chart (e.g. a Gattegno chart) or with place-value counters, add or remove ONE counter in the chosen column per step and read the whole number.

Say the count structurally too, keeping the unchanged places fixed: '46 ten-thousands and 2 thousand, 47 ten-thousands and 2 thousand, 48 ten-thousands and 2 thousand...' so only the ten-thousands count ticks while the 2,000 stays put.
Repeat for a different power of ten (e.g. count back in 100,000s from 800,000: 700,000 → 600,000 → 500,000) and name the column that now ticks.
activities.intendedInsight: Counting in a power of ten means repeatedly nudging a SINGLE place-value column up or down while every other digit stays frozen, as long as no boundary is crossed; the chosen step decides which column ticks. (When a column rolls over, e.g. 492,000 → 502,000, a neighbouring column changes too. This is covered in the boundary activity.)

activities.title: Crossing the boundary: the roll-over cascade
feedback: If 492,000 + 10,000 is given as 4,102,000 or the learner stalls, rehearse just the crossing: there are ten ten-thousands in one hundred-thousand, so the ten-thousands digit rolls from 9 back to 0 and the hundred-thousands increases by one, giving 502,000. Do not reteach the whole count — only rehearse boundaries.

If counting back stalls at a boundary (e.g. counting back in 10,000s from 502,000), pause at the crossing and ask which column must drop: the hundred-thousands digit decreases by one and the ten-thousands digit rolls back from 0 to 9, giving 492,000.

If the carry is applied to the wrong column, re-run the step slowly on the chart so each roll-over and carry is seen one column at a time (one carry for 492,000 → 502,000; two cascading carries for 990,000 → 1,000,000).
activities.rationale: Boundary roll-overs are the most common failure point and the place where the structure is most visible; isolating and rehearsing the crossing targets the error directly while keeping the single-column rule intact. A number line of equal power-of-ten hops and a chart showing the cascading carry make the mechanism concrete.
sourceClaims: Counting in powers of ten changes one place at a time with boundary roll-overs, best shown on a Gattegno chart/number line.
Year 5 pupils should 'count forwards or backwards in steps of powers of 10 for any given number up to 1,000,000'.
learnerActions: Count on in 10,000s and deliberately approach a boundary: 472,000 → 482,000 → 492,000 → 502,000, pausing at the crossing.
At 492,000, answer 'how many ten-thousands make the next hundred-thousand?' before stepping, then bridge to 502,000 and read the new hundred-thousands digit.
Count on in 10,000s up from 990,000 and watch the ten-thousands roll 9→0 while a carry cascades into the hundred-thousands and then the millions, reaching 1,000,000.

Count back in 10,000s across a boundary (522,000 → 512,000 → 502,000 → 492,000 → 482,000), noticing that at 502,000 → 492,000 the ten-thousands digit rolls back from 0 to 9 and the hundred-thousands digit decreases by one.
Predict a crossing before taking the step, then check: does only the next column change, or does the carry cascade further?
activities.intendedInsight: When a column fills, the single-column rule does not break — it cascades: counting forwards, the full column rolls over (9→0) and a carry moves into the next column, sometimes through several columns up to 1,000,000; counting backwards, an empty column rolls back (0→9) and the next column decreases by one.

activities.title: Spot the step and predict the next terms
feedback: If the step is misread, line up corresponding digits of two terms and ask which single column changed and by how much.
If next terms break the step size, restate the step and check each new term changes only the named column (unless a boundary forces a cascade).
For 375,000; 475,000; 575,000, confirm the step is +100,000 and the next term is 675,000; if a learner gives a non-constant step, compare each gap explicitly.
activities.rationale: Having children predict next terms and articulate the rule turns fluency into structural reasoning and lets secure learners meet boundary cases in a reasoning context. Continuing and predicting sequences cleanly works the generalised pattern of counting forwards and backwards in powers of ten.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should 'count forwards or backwards in steps of powers of 10 for any given number up to 1,000,000'.
learnerActions: Look at an unlabelled sequence such as 375,000; 475,000; 575,000 and work out the step by comparing consecutive terms (here +100,000).
State the step as a power of ten and which column changes, then write or say the next three terms (675,000; 775,000; 875,000).
Try sequences that cross a boundary so a prediction requires a roll-over, e.g. continue counting on in 10,000s from 472,000 through 502,000.
Make and swap sequences with a partner: hide the upcoming terms and have them predict, then articulate the rule in words.
For a backwards sequence, confirm the terms decrease and name the changing column.
activities.intendedInsight: The counting pattern becomes reasoning: identifying a constant power-of-ten step lets you justify and predict any later term, including across boundaries.

constraints: Reading a count on a static annotated chart or choosing the next term from fixed options can serve as a reference or check, but recognition-only responses do not elicit the independent counting and roll-over handling that is the objective; learners should generate the counts themselves aloud, in writing, or by acting on a chart/counters.
Keep the step size constant within any one count; mixing step sizes mid-count is a separate, harder task and should be flagged, not assumed.
Always state the direction (forwards/backwards) explicitly so decreasing counts are not accidentally incremented.
Boundary crossings (e.g. 492,000 → 502,000; 990,000 → 1,000,000) are the key difficulty and must be practised deliberately, not left to chance.

Interactive examples (a step selector with one highlighted column that ticks, an animated carry cascade, a number-line toggle of equal power-of-ten hops, a hidden-term prediction mode) are optional ways to make the single-column mechanism concrete; they are helpful illustrations, not required equipment, and equivalent work can be done with a paper chart, counters, and spoken counting.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Of the cited sources, the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified; the CCSS 4.NBT.1 and NCETM Primary Mastery claims are marked unverified in the source row and should be checked before relying on them.

The original material framed dialogue and 3D models as poor fits and a static chart as merely 'possible'. These catalog-style rankings have been removed; a conversation can still support articulating the rule and a fixed chart can still teach as a reference, so no universal 'only an interactive can teach this' claim is asserted.
The legacy error example '492,000 + 10,000 = 4,102,000' is retained only as a learner MISCONCEPTION to diagnose and correct (correct answer 502,000); it is never presented as a valid result.

The structural reading '46 ten-thousands' for 462,000 is a UK-mastery shorthand that, taken literally, equals 460,000; the activity keeps the fixed 2,000 explicit so the whole number is read correctly while the ticking digit is highlighted.

probeDeeper: Which digit changes each time you count on, and which stay still — until when?
What happens at 492,000 when you add one more ten-thousand — why does another column change?
If we counted back in ten-thousands from 502,000, what would we say?
In 375,000; 475,000; 575,000 — how did you work out the step?

errorPatterns.pattern: Adjusts the wrong place value — counts on in ten-thousands but changes the thousands or hundred-thousands digit (462,000 → 472,000 becomes 463,000 or 562,000).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to the ten-thousands column on a place-value chart and count with only that digit changing; say the count as '46 ten-thousands, 47 ten-thousands...'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The wrong column moves each step; the step size is not a constant ten-thousand.

errorPatterns.pattern: Can count in the unit on the flat but fails at the boundary — 492,000 + 10,000 is given as 4,102,000 or the child stalls, not rolling the ten-thousands into the hundred-thousands.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold just the crossing — pause at 492,000, ask 'how many ten-thousands make the next hundred-thousand?', bridge to 502,000; do not reteach the whole count, only rehearse boundaries.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Counting is smooth until a place rolls over, then breaks at 492,000 → 502,000 (or 800,000 counting back through 500,000).

responseLevels.gap: Changes the wrong place value or cannot sustain the count; step size is not constant.
responseLevels.full: Counts on and back in the given power of ten fluently, rolls places over correctly at boundaries, and identifies the step in an unlabelled sequence.
responseLevels.partial: Counts on/back in the unit correctly on the flat but breaks or stalls when a place rolls over at a boundary.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Count on out loud. (1) Start at 462,000 and count on in ten-thousands: 462,000... keep going for five more. (2) Start at 800,000 and count back in hundred-thousands. (3) A sequence goes 375,000; 475,000; 575,000 — what is the step, and what comes next?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watch what changes as they count. A child who understands the unit changes only the ten-thousands digit and rolls the next place at the boundary (492,000 → 502,000). A child adjusting the wrong place will say 462,000 → 463,000 or 562,000; a child without boundary understanding will stall or say 492,000 → 492,000-something / 4,102,000 when the ten-thousands rolls over.
